svg.text: Two networks, same species and connectance — very different structure
rows = prey · columns = predators · filled cell = "column species eats row species" · S = 20, C ≈ 0.10
1 basal species · links scattered across network
8 basal species · many species share similar diets → high redundancy
Each bar = one structural dimension · σ₁ largest → most important · zero bars = rank deficiency
σ₁ through σ₂₀ (4 zeros at right, rank = 16)

svg.text: Step 2 — rank and redundancy of diet strategies
Each column = one predator's diet vector · similar or zero columns reduce rank
Most columns unique (1 basal = 1 zero col)
8 basal cols zero + many similar diet patterns
Random placement → each predator has a unique diet pattern
Only 1 basal species (1 zero col) reduces rank slightly
8 zero cols + shared patterns among non-zero cols → rank = 9
8 basal species (zero cols) + many predators sharing similar diets → high structural redundancy
Higher D = more redundant diet strategies = more linearly dependent columns in the adjacency matrix
Note: both networks have the same S = 20 and C ≈ 0.10 — differences in metrics arise purely from structural organization
